reconcile.connective: The clearest resolution: apostles and prophets are foundations only in a secondary, ministerial sense, while Christ remains the sole true Foundation.

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells's Skeptic's Annotated Bible reads the two texts as flatly opposed: one names Jesus alone as foundation, the other names the apostles and prophets.

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.work: The Skeptic's Annotated Bible, "Foundation of the Church" (skepticsannotatedbible.com/contra/foundation.html)
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, The Skeptic's Annotated Bible (online; contra/foundation.html)

excerpts.excerpt_text: Christ Himself, the only true Foundation, was the grand subject of their ministry, and spring of their life. As one with Him and His fellow workers, they, too, in a secondary sense, are called "foundations" (Rev 21:14).
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: JFB directly answers the tension by grading two senses of 'foundation': Christ alone is the only true Foundation (matching 1 Cor 3:11's exclusivity), while the apostles/prophets are called 'foundations' only in a secondary, derivative sense (explaining Eph 2:20's wording).

pd_work.resource: John Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874)
pd_work.author: John Haley
pd_work.note: Haley treats this exact pairing under the heading 'The Foundation. Men are foundations.' (pp. 129-130): he argues the Ephesians phrase does not mean the apostles and prophets were themselves the foundation, but rather 'the foundation which pertained to them, — their foundation' (citing Meyer, Ellicott, Alford, and Bucer to the same effect), while Christ remains 'after all, the deep substructure, the foundation, of the church itself.'

link.title: 1 Corinthians 3:11—Who is the foundation of the church, Christ or the apostles?
link.note: live apologetic treatment; states the same primary/secondary-sense distinction as Haley and JFB ("Christ is the foundation in a primary sense, and His chosen apostles are the foundation in a secondary sense").
